entry.evidence: no systematic assessment of future changes under common climate change scenarios

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: The authors take from their own earlier glacio-hydrological work the finding that APHRODITE precipitation must be corrected upward to match discharge and glacier mass balance.
steps.quote: has to be corrected by factors of 1.2–4.3 at the catchment average

steps.action: They pose the open question of how glaciers and discharge in the five Tarim headwater catchments will change under common climate scenarios, and state the aim of a first systematic two-model assessment.
steps.quote: no systematic assessment of future changes under common climate change scenarios

steps.action: They assemble existing preprocessed datasets to drive, calibrate and validate the models: APHRODITE precipitation, WATCH climate, SRTM, land cover, soils, glacier outlines and thickness, and yearbook discharge.
steps.quote: mostly preprocessed (homogenised, synthesised) datasets are used in this study

steps.action: They adopt two glacio-hydrological models built in their earlier work: SWIM-G, with a glacier dynamics module on semi-distributed units, and WASA, as applied to Central Asian catchments.
steps.quote: that was recently extended by a glacier dynamics module

steps.action: SWIM-G is calibrated by multi-objective Pareto optimisation against discharge, glacier area hypsometry and mass balance, with a 300-year glacier spin-up; the best trade-off parameter set is chosen.
steps.quote: using a multi-objective Pareto optimisation with three objective functions

steps.action: Scenario runs are repeated with the best and worst SWIM-G parameter sets, and an ANOVA partitions variance among climate models, scenario and parameter set.
steps.quote: the scenarios were also run with the best/worst parameter sets and an analysis of variance

steps.action: WASA is calibrated to daily discharge for Hotan and Yarkant (1979–1988), with glacier mass loss constrained near balance; the Aksu calibration is taken from Duethmann et al. (2015).
steps.quote: the mass loss was constrained to 0 ± 0.1 m w.eq. a−1

steps.action: WASA is evaluated on held-out periods (1972–1978 for Hotan and Yarkant; 1957–1975 and 2000–2004 for Aksu), with validation Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.71–0.84.
steps.quote: The period 1972–1978 was used for model evaluation.

steps.action: The scenario experiment is designed as three RCPs crossed with eight CMIP5 GCMs, chosen to span the ensemble's range of warmer/colder and wetter/drier signals.
steps.quote: The models were selected to cover the full range of precipitation and temperature change signals from the CMIP5 ensemble

steps.action: GCM output is bias-adjusted to the calibration driving data with trend-preserving quantile mapping, which the authors justify despite published concerns about bias adjustment.
steps.quote: A non-parametric quantile mapping approach with trend preservation was chosen

steps.action: Bias-adjusted ensemble projections of temperature and precipitation are analysed per catchment and period, showing warmer and mostly wetter conditions.
steps.quote: Increases in both temperature and precipitation are projected under most climate scenarios

steps.action: Both models project glacier area, volume and mass balance per catchment under each RCP; recession strengthens with scenario.
steps.quote: A receding trend over the twenty-first century is evident in all catchments for the ensemble medians of both models

steps.action: The glacier projections of SWIM-G and WASA are compared; they differ in magnitude by region (WASA loses more in Aksu, SWIM-G more in Hotan and Yarkant).
steps.quote: WASA simulates a much stronger decline of glacier areas in the Aksu basin than SWIM-G

steps.action: Annual and monthly discharge changes are projected and traced to runoff components (rain, snowmelt, glacier melt): Aksu discharge peaks early then recedes, while Hotan and Yarkant discharge increases.
steps.quote: In the two Aksu subcatchments, the increase in mean annual discharge is most pronounced in the near future

steps.action: The projected discharge increase is set against observed past trends, and the basin-wide peak-water timing of global studies is attributed mainly to the Aksu.
steps.quote: Results indicate a marked increase in river discharge, which is in-line with observations over the past decades

steps.action: Agreement between the two models is assessed: they share the direction of glacier and discharge change except Aksu far-future discharge.
steps.quote: Both models generally agree on the direction of glacial and discharge changes

steps.action: Inter-model differences are proposed to arise from different precipitation corrections and evapotranspiration, and from different ice representations (glacier dynamics, sublimation, debris); these explanations are not tested.
steps.quote: predominantly caused by different assumptions in the precipitation correction

steps.action: ANOVA results are reported: parameter-set variance is under 20% of total discharge variance and the climate-model ensemble over 50%; the WASA ANOVA is taken from Duethmann et al. (2016).
steps.quote: the variance related to different parameter sets amounts to less than 20% of the total

steps.action: The projections are kept with scenario ranges for temperature, precipitation, glacier shrinkage and discharge per headwater region.
steps.quote: the models project river discharge to mainly increase in the Hotan and Yarkant catchments by the end of the century

tree.answer: Future climate-driven change in glaciers and discharge of the Tarim headwaters
No; future state, reachable only through calibrated models forced by GCM scenarios
Projection of 21st-century glacier and runoff change with its uncertainty
No stated rival hypotheses; three RCPs, eight GCMs and two impact models span the uncertainty
Conditions set in silico by scenario forcing of calibrated models
Direction of change holds across two models (except Aksu far-future discharge); parameter variance under 20% versus climate-model variance over 50%
Projections kept with scenario and ensemble ranges

end.claim: Under RCP 2.6/4.5/8.5, glacier cover is projected to shrink by about 45/52/73% in the Aksu and 21/28/40% in the Hotan and Yarkant headwaters by 2071–2100; Aksu discharge first rises about 20% then returns to or below reference, while Hotan and Yarkant discharge rises by about 15/30/60%.

decisive_move.sentence: Forcing two calibrated glacio-hydrological models with bias-adjusted output of eight GCMs under three RCPs produces the glacier and discharge projections that constitute the claim.

gates.evidence: All data were pre-existing compiled datasets; no hypothesis directed acquisition (§3.1 ¶1). The models faced calibration and held-out validation tests they could have failed (§3.2.1 ¶2; §3.2.2 ¶2), but the projections themselves cannot be tested against outcomes. Nothing was fixed in advance; GCM selection and bias adjustment were chosen during the work (§3.3 ¶1–¶2).

imports.item: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) to partition projection uncertainty
Multi-objective Pareto optimisation for model calibration
Non-parametric trend-preserving quantile mapping for bias adjustment

novelty_claims.quote: This study aims to provide a first systematic climate change impact assessment for the twenty-first century of the Tarim River headwaters
This study represents the first systematic and comprehensive climate change impact assessment of the Tarim River headwater catchments for the twenty-first century

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so only a final_paper sequence is coded. The supplementary Annexes (Tables A1–A4, Figures A2–A8) were not supplied; ANOVA and calibration details there are unseen. The paper cites the SWIM-G ANOVA as Figure A8 (§3.2.1 ¶2) and as Figure A5 (§5 ¶5), an inconsistency. The split between calibration done here and calibration inherited (Wortmann et al. 2018 for SWIM-G; Duethmann et al. 2015 for WASA Aksu) is unclear; step 5 is coded as new by inference. SWIM-G validation within 1961–1987 does not state a held-out period, so its replication entry is inference. The first row of Table 1 in the PDF repeats the Kaqun values under a header label, apparently a typesetting error. Claim status: the projections are coded estimate_with_resolution for want of a projection category; they are scenario-conditional and not scored against outcomes. Composition none_fits: a calibrate-then-project ensemble with no rival tested and no frozen forecast verified, so neither forecast_verification nor trace_series applies. Sub-claims: (a) inter-model differences arise from precipitation correction, evapotranspiration and ice representation (hypothesis, untested, status none); (b) glacio-hydrological modelling is a suitable route to high-elevation precipitation estimates (suggested, inherited from earlier work, status none here); (c) basin-wide peak-water timing in global studies reflects mainly the Aksu (best_explanation, by comparison only).

disagreements.target: Huss and Hock (2018); Rounce et al. (2020), basin-wide Tarim peak-water timing
disagreements.support: Catchment-resolved projections show the early peak in the Aksu, while Hotan and Yarkant peak only in the medium to far future.
disagreements.quote: these projected peaks for the whole basin can mainly be attributed to the Asku basin as Hotan and Yarkand show a distinctly different behaviour

disagreements.target: Ehret et al. (2012), concerns about bias-correcting climate model data
disagreements.support: The authors argue bias adjustment is necessary here because of large precipitation deviations and the glaciers' sensitivity to small climatic differences; no comparison without adjustment is shown.
disagreements.quote: Despite concerns of the validity of using a bias-adjustment for climate change impact assessments (Ehret et al. 17), it was considered necessary

disagreements.target: APHRODITE gridded precipitation (Yatagai et al. 2012) and other observation-based precipitation products
disagreements.support: Their earlier glacio-hydrological modelling showed catchment precipitation underestimated by factors of 1.2–4.3, so corrected precipitation is used.
disagreements.quote: which introduces an underestimation in catchment-wide precipitation interpolations

alternatives_considered.chosen: SWIM-G parameter set with the best trade-off between all objective functions
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Other non-dominated Pareto parameter sets, including the best/worst sets
alternatives_considered.reason: offers the best trade-off between all objective functions

alternatives_considered.chosen: Most plausible mass balance scenario for SWIM-G calibration in Hotan and Yarkant
alternatives_considered.reason: long-term mass balance measurements were not available

alternatives_considered.chosen: One WASA solution from the Pareto set
Semi-distributed computational units (elevation, aspect, subbasin) in SWIM-G
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Gridded (fully distributed) or empirical glacier approaches
alternatives_considered.reason: to overcome the conflict of scale between individual glaciers and catchment hydrology

alternatives_considered.chosen: Non-parametric quantile mapping with trend preservation
alternatives_considered.alternatives: No bias adjustment (per Ehret et al. concerns)
alternatives_considered.reason: considerable precipitation deviations between calibration and scenario data, and great sensitivity of glacier cover

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Other precipitation datasets compared in Wortmann et al. (2018); interpolated station data (used for WASA in Aksu)
alternatives_considered.reason: best data available; densest gauge network in Asia
